newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai Cable TV plans expansion, new services.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai Cable TV plans expansion, new services.

text.p: Shanghai's Cable Television network, the largest in China, is planning to reach three million households, or 75 percent of the city's population, by 2000, the station head said on Wednesday.

Hu Yunchou, the network's president, said in an interview the station also planned to boost signal power from the current 450 megahertz to 750 megahertz by the end of the century, making it possible for the system to handle hundreds of channels.
"We are aiming to hit three million households by the year 2000, or about 75-80 percent of the market," said Hu.

Like all media in China, the network is state-run and sees its main responsibility as "contributing to the reform process". But it makes a profit too, Hu said, although he declined to give any profit details.

The network currently carries 18 channels -- eight of them re-transmissions from China Central Television in Beijing, five of them local broadcast channels and five channels run by Shanghai Cable TV channel itself.
Shanghai Cable TV started operations in 1992 and hit 1.8 million households by the end of last year, out of a total for greater Shanghai of around 4.4 million households.

Each household pays 240 yuan (US$29) for installation of the cable service and then a monthly fee of eight yuan ($1). Four scrambled channels from Beijing can be viewed on payment of an extra five yuan.

"We have plans to expand the range of channels to include focussed programming for children, the elderly, for education. We are looking at a shopping channel and we are doing tests on video on demand," Hu said.
The Chinese government bans the use of satellite dishes by private individuals and has promoted cable networks as a means of slowing the penetration of satellite television, analysts say.
"Much of the programming on the satellite channels does not meet the needs of the country and does not match the Spiritual Civilization standard," Hu said.
Spiritual Civilization is the title of a public morality campaign promoted in recent years by the ruling Chinese Communist Party.
The channel's advertising revenue in 1996 was 200 million yuan, up from 120 million yuan in 1995, with a further big increase of 25 percent to 250 million yuan expected in 1997, Hu said.
"The trend is very positive for us, and for other broadcast media as well," he said.

He said the quality of Shanghai Cable TV's own programming was somewhat lower than that of the local broadcast channels, but the channel's top audience-grabbing programmes -- serial dramas -- sometimes took 35-40 percent of the Shanghai viewership.

Advertising rates are growing as the network and viewership expands. Hu said a 30-second prime time slot on the station cost 16,000 yuan, up from 12,000 last year, but still dramatically lower than the 30,000 yuan charged by the broadcast channels.

Hu said that unlike many cable systems in other parts of China, Shanghai Cable does not carry satellite channels, although it has an agreement with U.S. sports network ESPN for the use of its programming on Shanghai Cable's sports channel.

He said national policy forbade the re-transmission of foreign satellite channels, but the policy on satellite channels emanating from Hong Kong after the colony's handover to China on July 1 was unclear.
